verdict: OK to lend in Panipat carpets and rugs, but only to fire-compliant, powerloom-backed units with verified export order books; avoid units with uninsured plant, water-dependent processing and stretched working capital.
title: Panipat Carpets & Rugs: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
Panipat turns yarn into rugs and blankets on powerlooms, then finishes, packs and ships to export buyers and domestic wholesale. **Cash is made in the finishing and order-book stage, not at the loom** — the loom is cheap, the dyeing, washing and packing line is where money sits. The working-capital cycle is long: yarn and cotton inventory must be carried ahead of the season, and export receivables run well past the shipment date. **So when a proposal lands, check the inventory days and receivable days separately; if receivables exceed the buyer credit period you have been shown, ask for the buyer-wise ageing.**

## What has changed now
Two local facts matter. A blanket factory in Balana village caught fire and a wall collapsed, with workers escaping narrowly [1] — **fire safety and insurance are now a live credit issue, not a compliance box**. Separately, the handloom industry is openly looking at shifting to Uttar Pradesh amid water shortage and NCR-related pressure [2][3]. **So when a proposal lands, check the fire NOC, the insurer's reinstatement value and the water source; if the unit depends on purchased tanker water, ask for the last twelve months of water cost and treat it as a margin risk.** Peer results are mixed: Faze Three grew revenue 32.92% to ₹932.76 crore in FY26 but operating profit fell 20.15% to ₹42.04 crore [5]; Welspun Living reported Q4 FY26 EBITDA margin of 10.8% [7] and is targeting UK and US demand with H2 capex of INR 3.5 billion [6]. **Read this as volume growth without pricing power — so do not lend against a margin story, lend against the order book.**

## Where the growth is
Haryana GST collections rose 10.1% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1% [D], and India-wide IIP for NIC 13 output rose 13.1% YoY [D]. **Pursue the mid-sized powerloom unit with a real export buyer list and its own finishing line; avoid the pure job-work loom with one buyer and no finishing.** The Oriental Weavers 9M 2024 presentation shows total revenue up 34% with a 16.6% EBITDA margin [4] — that is an Egyptian market number, not Indian, and it is old; use it only as a shape, not a benchmark.

## How to grow safely
Structure term loans against the finishing line, not against land. **Take monthly stock statements, monthly buyer-wise sales and the insurance premium receipt every quarter; if stock cover falls below the drawing power you have sanctioned, freeze further disbursement.** For export-backed units, insist on ECGC cover or a confirmed letter of credit. Marwar Carpets ran working capital limits around 80% utilised for twelve months with cash of 0.22 crore as on March 31, 2022 [10] — **that is the profile to decline, not to price higher.**

## Early warning signs
Watch for a shift of looms to Uttar Pradesh [2][3], rising water purchase cost, and any factory without a current fire NOC [1]. **If a borrower's power bill falls while sales stay flat, ask where the looms went.** Collect from customer: current water cost per unit, fire insurance reinstatement value, and buyer-wise receivable ageing.
